Rapid identification of virulence- and resistance-associated genes is therefore essential for early diagnosis, antimicrobial stewardship, and infection control. In this study, we developed a smartphone-assisted one-tube enzymatic recombinase amplification (ERA)-CRISPR/Cas12a biosensor for simultaneous detection of four hvKP-associated virulence genes (iroB, iucA, peg-344, and rmpA) and two clinically important resistance genes (bla<sub>NDM-1</sub> and mcr-1). To overcome the aerosol contamination risk typical of conventional CRISPR diagnostics, our platform features an innovative sealed dual-chamber reaction tube that physically isolates ERA amplification from CRISPR/Cas12a cleavage until manually punctured. The biosensor demonstrates high analytical sensitivity with a limit of detection (LOD) of 1 × 10<sup>1</sup> CFU/mL and can be fully completed within 45 min under isothermal conditions (42 °C). Furthermore, a custom portable fluorescence detector wirelessly transmits real-time data to a smartphone application for immediate analysis. Importantly, the biosensor exhibited 100% positive agreement with standard qPCR when evaluating blood samples from a mouse infection model and a diverse cohort of 76 clinical K. pneumoniae isolates. Overall, this portable, highly sensitive, and contamination-controlled biosensor provides a robust point-of-care testing (POCT) platform for the rapid screening of multidrug-resistant hvKP.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0740-0020(26)00192-9</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in dairy production represents an important One Health concern, particularly in countries with predominantly small-scale farms and limited AMR surveillance in livestock. This cross-sectional study investigated the herd-level prevalence of selected antibiotic-resistant bacteria in bulk tank milk (BTM) from 100 conventional dairy farms across seven districts in Serbia and evaluated associations with farm management practices. Samples were screened for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)- and AmpC beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli, carbapenemase-producing E. coli (CPE), colistin-resistant E. coli (ColR-E), and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp. (VRE). Isolates from selective media were identified and characterized using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF), antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and PCR-based confirmation of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). Farm management data were collected through structured questionnaires and analysed using logistic and Firth's penalised regression models. MRSA was confirmed on five farms and ESBL E. coli on four farms, while VRE, CPE, and ColR-E were not detected. All confirmed MRSA and ESBL E. coli isolates carried the corresponding ARGs, and most isolates were multidrug-resistant (MDR). While most farm management variables showed no significant association with antibiotic-resistant bacteria, higher average daily milk production per cow was significantly linked to ESBL E. coli prevalence. Although the overall AMR prevalence was low, the detection of MDR strains highlights the importance of continued surveillance. BTM analysis proved to be a practical tool for farm-level AMR monitoring and may inform targeted antimicrobial stewardship strategies across countries, including the dairy sector in Serbia.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 The Authors. ValidYN="Y">10.1080/17441692.2026.2742514</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most consequential threats to global public health. In 2021, bacterial AMR was associated with an estimated 4.71 million deaths globally, including 1.14 million directly attributable to resistance. Yet, despite its designation as a global emergency, policy responses remain heavily focused on surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, diagnostics, and pharmaceutical innovation. These interventions are necessary but insufficient without sustained action on the social and structural conditions shaping infection exposure, access to care, and antibiotic use. This commentary argues that the One Health framework, as currently operationalised, does not sufficiently centre poverty and structural inequality as core determinants of AMR. AMR is shaped by overcrowded living conditions, inadequate water and sanitation, disrupted health systems, weak diagnostic infrastructure, gender inequities, and unreliable access to quality-assured medicines, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). We propose four linked policy directions: aligning national AMR action plans with the Sustainable Development Goals; integrating socioeconomic disaggregation into AMR surveillance; reforming international financing to expand fiscal space for health, WASH, and diagnostics; and embedding communities as co-designers of stewardship and governance. A justice-oriented One Health approach is essential to translate global AMR commitments into equitable and durable action.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author ValidYN="Y">10.1080/19932820.2026.2713956</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Inappropriate antibiotic use in community settings is a major contributor to antimicrobial resistance, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where regulatory enforcement may be inconsistent. Community pharmacies are a critical interface between health systems and the public; however, real-world dispensing practices remain insufficiently characterized in many settings. This study evaluated the prevalence, behavioral drivers, and clinical quality of non-prescription antibiotic dispensing in Jordanian community pharmacies using a simulated patient methodology.A cross-sectional simulated patient study was conducted across 200 community pharmacies in Jordan. A standardized encounter involving a three-stage progressive escalation protocol assessed dispensing behavior under increasing patient demand. The primary outcome was antibiotic supply without a valid prescription. Secondary outcomes included clinical assessment, counseling, referral behavior, and antibiotic class supplied. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of non-prescription dispensing and adequate clinical assessment.Antibiotics were dispensed without prescription in 162 encounters (81.0%; 95% CI, 75.6-86.4). During the initial symptom-based presentation, 110 pharmacies (55.0%) supplied antibiotics. Among pharmacies that initially declined, a direct antibiotic request resulted in additional dispensing in 44.4% of cases, while subsequent patient insistence led to further supply in 24.0%, producing a cumulative prevalence of 81.0%. Independent pharmacies (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 2.48; 95% CI, 1.23-5.02) and rural locations (AOR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.01-4.03) were associated with higher dispensing odds. History-taking occurred in 49.4% of dispensing encounters, allergy screening in 14.2%, and no counseling was provided in 29.0%. Broad-spectrum agents represented 73.5% of dispensed antibiotics.Non-prescription antibiotic dispensing remains widespread in Jordan and is influenced by patient pressure and practice characteristics. Strengthened regulatory enforcement, professional training, and public awareness interventions are urgently needed.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author Urinary tract infections (UTIs) frequently require antibiotics, yet inappropriate prescribing remains high.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="OBJECTIVE" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">To assess how a structured audit process, supported by information technology (IT), influences antibiotic prescribing practices for UTIs in the Urology Department at Prime Hospital.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="DESIGN" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">A 12-month quasi-experimental study was conducted in two phases: preintervention and intervention. A customized module in the electronic medical record (EMR) system monitored UTI prescriptions. Alerts for restricted antibiotics were reviewed daily by the antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) team, with immediate feedback to prescribers. The audit emphasized adherence to empirical guidelines, reducing fluoroquinolone use, promoting Access group antibiotics, and minimizing restricted agents.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="PATIENTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">All adult UTI patients in the Urology Department were included; pediatric patients under 12 and pregnant women were excluded.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">The intervention improved guideline adherence increased the use of Access group antibiotics and reduced restricted antibiotic prescriptions by approximately 50%. Daily multidisciplinary feedback reinforced rational prescribing; however, sustaining long-term behavioral change remained challenging.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Despite growing awareness of AMR, inappropriate antibiotic use persists. IT-enabled audits, combined with multidisciplinary collaboration, effectively enhance guideline adherence, promote rational antibiotic use, and improve patient care outcomes in hospital-based UTI This study investigated the bacterial etiology, antimicrobial resistance profiles, and associated risk factors among elderly patients presenting with diarrhea at an urban Kenyan referral hospital.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 271 patients aged ≥60 years presenting with acute diarrhea at Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, Nairobi, between February and December 2025. Stool specimens were cultured using selective and differential media, and bacterial isolates were identified by standard biochemical methods. <i>Escherichia coli</i> isolates were identified biochemically only, and pathotyping was not determined, so their contribution to the diarrheal illness reported here cannot be established with certainty. <i>Clostridioides difficile</i> was confirmed on isolates recovered by anaerobic culture, using glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen and toxin A/B immunoassays performed on colony suspensions rather than directly on unprocessed stool. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion (Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [CLSI] M100, 35th edition) and Etest methods, with organism-specific interpretive criteria applied only where validated for the organism tested.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Potential enteric bacterial isolates were recovered from 118 of 271 participants (43.5%); this falls to 84/271 (31.0%) if untyped <i>E. coli</i> is excluded from the numerator, since its causal role in the presenting illness could not be confirmed without pathotyping. <i>E. coli</i> was the most frequently recovered isolate (28.8%), followed by <i>C. difficile</i> (15.3%), <i>Campylobacter jejuni</i> (10.2%), and <i>Shigella flexneri</i> (8.5%). Among the 80 isolates belonging to organisms with validated, organism-specific disk-diffusion interpretive criteria (<i>i.e.</i>, excluding <i>C. difficile</i>,.<i>C jejuni</i>, and organisms lacking a validated breakpoint standard for the panel used), and after excluding categories representing intrinsic rather than acquired resistance, the pooled multidrug resistance (MDR) prevalence was 62.5% (50/80). <i>Salmonella typhi</i> demonstrated 100% MDR (8/8); <i>Klebsiella pneumoniae</i> showed an MDR rate of 66.7% (2/3) after its intrinsic ampicillin resistance was excluded, and <i>E. coli</i> 70.6% (24/34). <i>C. jejuni</i> showed extensive non-susceptibility across the same six-agent panel (9/12 isolates non-susceptible in ≥3 categories), but because disk diffusion is not validated by CLSI or European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing for this organism, these findings are reported separately as exploratory, epidemiological data only and were excluded from the pooled MDR estimate and from clinical interpretation. No significant associations were identified between infection status and water, sanitation, hygiene, or dietary factors (<i>P</i> ≥ 0.85 for all comparisons).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Elderly patients in urban Kenya carry a substantial burden of enteric bacterial isolates with high rates of MDR among the organisms for which resistance could be validly classified. Because many bacterial diarrheal illnesses are self-limiting and do not require antimicrobial therapy, these findings support selective, culture- and susceptibility-guided prescribing rather than blanket empirical antibiotic use. Strengthened antimicrobial stewardship, expanded diagnostic and pathotyping capacity, and integration of elderly populations into diarrheal disease surveillance programs are The survey explored the respondents' sociodemographic data, antibiotic knowledge, AMR awareness, and behavioral intentions in common clinical scenarios. Statistical analysis evaluated knowledge, attitudes, and practices scores by education level, academic background, and geographic region.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Respondents were predominantly from Asia and Africa. Higher education levels overall and a science background in particular were strongly associated with higher knowledge and more positive attitudes (<i>P</i> < 0.001). However, only 38% knew that antibiotics treat bacterial infections. Over half expected antibiotics for cold or flu symptoms; 31% would question why doctors were not prescribing them, and 18.5% would seek a second opinion. Awareness of the impact of antibiotics on the gut microbiome and fetal health was linked to reduced antibiotic-seeking behavior.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">The findings primarily reflect engagement from the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent. The critical gaps in the public's understanding of appropriate antibiotic use support the need for school- and university-based AMR curricula, greater community engagement, and strategic use of The most recent antibiotic course within the preceding 6 months was the index course. Self-medication was defined by the absence of prescribing involvement from a Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council-registered physician. Design-aware modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios, accounting for clustering and stratification. Self-medicated antibiotics were classified using the World Health Organization Access, Watch, and Reserve framework.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Self-medication occurred in 244/400 participants (61.0%; 95% confidence interval 55.6%-66.4%). Higher prevalence was associated with pharmacy access (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.50, 95% confidence interval 1.29-1.74), poor antibiotic knowledge (1.46, 1.24-1.73), lower educational attainment (1.30, 1.09-1.55), and lack of antimicrobial-resistance awareness (1.22, 1.06-1.41). Watch or Reserve agents accounted for 145/201 classifiable episodes (72.1%) and 117/152 objectively verified episodes (77.0%).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Antibiotic self-medication was common among recent antibiotic users. Pharmacy access and limited antimicrobial literacy were associated characteristics rather than demonstrated causal determinants. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) is a unique diagnostic tool; however, its effectiveness for high-risk populations remains unclear.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">This retrospective study included 642 ICU patients with pneumonia unresponsive to initial treatment, categorized into single- or repeat-test groups based on mNGS testing frequency. We analyzed the results of mNGS and conventional microbiological tests (CMTs), compared microbial detection characteristics between patients with different immune statuses, assessed the impact of repeat testing on microbial detection and treatment adjustments and evaluated its association with patient prognosis using multivariable logistic regression and propensity score matching.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Among 642 patients, patient-level agreement between mNGS and CMTs was low (κ = 0.180, <i>p</i> < 0.001). First bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF)-mNGS results showed a higher microbial detection rate in immunocompromised than immunocompetent patients. Among patients undergoing repeat BALF-mNGS testing, partial concordance between first and second tests was most common pattern. Antibiotic treatments were modified in 67.6% of cases based on mNGS results, with a higher adjustment rate in the repeat-test group. Although ICU mortality was higher in the repeat-test group, multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed no significant association between repeat testing and mortality risk (adjusted odds ratio = 1.15, 95% CI: 0.64-2.06, <i>p</i> = 0.630). After propensity score matching, no significant difference was observed between two groups (absolute risk difference: 1.12%, 95% CI: -7.43% to 9.67%, <i>p</i> = 0.798).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">mNGS is a valuable microbial detection tool for ICU patients with pneumonia unresponsive to initial treatment and can support early antimicrobial adjustment. Repeat testing can provide information on dynamic changes in the microbial spectrum during disease but was not associated with improved patient outcomes, suggesting that repeat testing frequency should be carefully considered to avoid unnecessary testing. mNGS results should be interpreted in conjunction with CMTs, host immune status and inflammatory biomarkers to optimise its clinical value in ICU pneumonia.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author Hence, this study conducted to assess the association between farm-level biosecurity practices and antimicrobial use in commercial poultry farms in Bangladesh. A cross-sectional study was conducted on 331 poultry farms (broiler: 113, layer: 103, Sonali: 115) across six districts from September to December 2021. A directed acyclic graph informed variable selection and generalized linear models (GLM) and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were used to identify factors associated with antimicrobial use. Overall, 27.8% of farms reported antibiotic use on the day of the interview, and 49.2% had used antibiotics in the preceding 14 days. Antimicrobial use was significantly higher in rural farms and those with dirt floors or floor-based rearing systems. Higher odds of antimicrobial use were also linked to farmer education level, proximity to recent avian influenza outbreaks, unrestricted access of wild animal, and nearby crow roost. Conversely, farms implementing stronger biosecurity including isolating sick birds, and farms rearing layer birds and maintaining improved infrastructure reported significantly lower antibiotic use. These findings indicate that farm infrastructure, wildlife interfaces and hygiene practices are important correlates of antimicrobial use. Strengthening farm-level biosecurity, regulating antimicrobial access, and expanding veterinary extension services, especially in rural areas are critical to reduce antibiotic dependency and mitigating AMR risks. Establishing a national AMR surveillance framework that links animal, environmental, and human health sectors is essential to monitor resistance patterns and guide targeted policy interventions.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© 2026 The Authors.
